newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS - NOV 25.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS - NOV 25.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek financial press:

--Firms investing in synthetic swaps will be exempt from new taxes on derivatives as long as their capital is used to protect against fluctuations in inflation or drachma parities, the national economy and finance ministry says.

--The budget and economic policy are now issues of national importance, National Economy and Finance Minister Alekos Papadopoulos tells the Ethnos newspaper. "There are no margins for retreat: this is our last chance," he stresses, adding that the "harshest budget in the last 15 years" is necessary for Greece's participation in economic and monetary union.

--The privatisations of ailing companies is on the cards again at the development ministry. A meeting is expected to evaluate the situation facing Softex, Kerafina, Elefsina Bauxite, MEL and Larco as well as AEBAL.

--A second brokerage firm defaults: checks on the Nikiforos Securities firm have found 300 million drachmas worth of missing shares as well as irregularities which are expected to increase this amount.
--Relations between the Commercial and Ionian Banks are reconsidered again as the national economy ministry feels conditions are ripe for an expansion of the Commercial Group.

--The development ministry is expected to pursue a "gentlement's agreement" with leading firms in the Greek market on a restrained pricing policy for 1997. Firms will be asked to keep price increases on products below 5.0 percent as part of the government's efforts to squeeze inflation. The ministry is expected to stress that the 'hard drachma' policy of recent years has significantly contributed to increased profits; a similarly restrained pricing policy is to be followed by public utilities and organisations (DEKO).

--The government is walking a fine line between political balances and economic necessities with the 1997 budget. Interestingly, the lion's share of projected state spending has gone to education and defence, both ministries run by the prime minister's main antagonists.

--Delta's default was only the tip of the iceberg, reports state, with each day bringing to light more problems in brokerage firms. Smaller firms are finding it difficult to keep pace with the new measures introduced by the Capital Market Commission, with a climate of restraint noted in transactions and banks accepting only bank cheques from brokerage firms.

--The 1997 budget is almost ready, with decisions having been taken on which taxation measures will be imposed and only the fine tuning remaining. The value of wealth indicators (cars, pleasure craft) have been readjusted downwards and extended to include second homes and home help. Various scenarios are being considered for the real estate tax but there will be no change to currently valid income brackets.

--A suit filed by the Athens bourse's clearing house alleges that certain Delta Securities stockholders and executives skimmed off some two billion drachmas. Meanwhile, a court investigation into the bourse scandal closes in on five brokerage firms and 10 investors.
--National Bank of Greece Governor Theodoros Karatzas says thje recent AGET-Heracles agreement with Italian firm Concretum has safeguarded the interests of Greek industry.

--The burden of development will be carried by infrastructure, Environment, Town Planning and Public Works Minister Costas Laliotis says. EWight of ten major projects are on course; the speeding up of public works projects will boost the building industry into playing a leading role in 1997. --Maria Petrakis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
